what_its_for: Bromfenac is a medicated eye drop used to treat pain and swelling (inflammation) in your eye after cataract surgery. It belongs to a group of medicines called NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) and works by blocking chemicals in your eye that cause pain and redness.
how_to_take: Use this medicine only in the eye — never swallow it. Wash your hands well before using. Tilt your head back, gently pull down your lower eyelid to make a small pocket, and place one drop into that pocket. Close your eye gently for about 2 minutes — do not blink hard or squeeze your eye shut. Press lightly on the inner corner of your eye (near your nose) with one finger for 1–2 minutes to help keep the drop in your eye. If you wear contact lenses, take them out before using bromfenac and wait at least 10 minutes before putting them back in. If you use other eye drops, wait at least 5 minutes between each different drop.
dosing: The usual dose is 1 drop in the affected eye(s) once a day. Start using it the day before your cataract surgery, use it again on the day of surgery, and then continue for 14 days after surgery. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — they may adjust how often you use it.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, use the drop as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not use 2 drops at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store bromfenac eye drops at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C and 25°C). Keep the bottle tightly closed when not in use. Keep it away from light, heat, and moisture. Do not freeze. Keep all medicines out of reach of children. Throw away the bottle 28 days after you first open it, even if there is still medicine left.
what_to_avoid: Do not touch the tip of the dropper to your eye, fingers, or any other surface — this can contaminate the drops and cause an eye infection. Avoid wearing soft contact lenses while you are being treated for eye inflammation after surgery unless your doctor says it is okay. Do not use bromfenac if you are allergic to aspirin or other NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen), as you may also be sensitive to this medicine. Avoid rubbing your eyes after using the drops.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you notice: increased eye pain, redness, or swelling that gets worse; changes in your vision or blurry vision; a feeling that something is in your eye that does not go away; crusting, discharge, or oozing from your eye; sensitivity to light that is getting worse; or any signs of an allergic reaction such as itching, rash, or severe eye irritation. Rare but serious side effects include damage to the surface of the eye — this is more likely if you use it longer than prescribed or if you have dry eyes, diabetes, or rheumatoid arthritis.
when_it_works: Bromfenac starts working to reduce inflammation soon after you begin using it. Most people notice less eye pain, redness, and discomfort within the first few days. It is important to use all the doses your doctor prescribed even if your eye feels better, to make sure healing is complete.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before using bromfenac if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It is generally not recommended during the last 3 months of pregnancy. Children: Safety and effectiveness in children have not been established. Older adults: No special dose adjustment is needed for older adults, but they should be monitored for any signs of eye irritation. Patients with bleeding problems or who take blood thinners: Tell your doctor, as bromfenac may slow blood clotting in eye tissues. Patients with corneal problems or dry eye disease: Use with extra caution and close monitoring, as bromfenac may worsen these conditions.
